title: Old match notes stop counting past 20%
allegory: PPO's clip is a coach's rule for a chess bot studying notes from its own old games: lean into the moves that worked, but once you play a move 20% more or less often than you did in those games, the old notes stop counting, because they no longer describe you.

chapters.name: Learning from stale games
chapters.note: aggression paid off ... in games I played timidly

cap.1: A chess bot plays a thousand games and notices aggression paid off. It keeps hammering that lesson in, still learning from its old timid games, and gets worse.
cap.2: PPO takes several gradient steps on each batch of rollouts. After the first step the policy has moved, so the batch describes a slightly different agent than the one learning.
cap.3: On-policy estimates go stale within a learning phase. Push far enough and you confidently optimise a surrogate that no longer applies to the current policy.

cap.1: A coach adds one rule: lean into what worked, but once you play a move 20% more or less often than in those games, the old notes stop counting.
cap.2: For each action, compare the new policy's probability with the old one's. The ratio starts at 1. Once it moves more than 20% either way, PPO stops giving credit.
cap.3: r_t = π_θ(a_t|s_t) / π_old(a_t|s_t), with θ_old frozen for the learning phase. ε = 0.2 in the paper and in ARENA's defaults (clip_coef=0.2).

cap.1: Two versions of the credit: as it stands and capped. Taking the smaller means you can never earn more by drifting further from how you used to play.
cap.2: torch.min(ratio * adv, ratio.clamp(1 - eps, 1 + eps) * adv).mean(), maximised. The min makes the cap bite only in the direction that would over-reward drift.
cap.3: For A above 0 the objective caps at (1+ε)A; for A below 0 it floors at (1-ε)A, so one update can't crush an action's probability. Outside the band the gradient is exactly 0.

cap.1: Credit against how much more often you now play a move. For a good move, credit stops rising past 1.2. For a bad move, the penalty stops growing below 0.8.
cap.2: For a good move the objective goes flat once r passes 1 + ε: no reason to push further. For a bad move it goes flat below 1 - ε: no crushing its probability in one go.
cap.3: Flat segments have zero gradient with respect to θ; the unclipped sides keep full slope. Since min(rA, clip(r)A) ≤ rA, the objective is a pessimistic bound on the unclipped one.

chapters.name: Not a KL penalty
chapters.verdict: TRPO is the one with an explicit KL constraint. Three mechanisms, often muddled.

cap.1: Don't mix up the coach's rule and a leash. PPO's rule is a hard cap against your last batch of games; RLHF adds a separate soft leash to a fixed start.
cap.2: PPO constrains by clipping the ratio against the policy that collected the batch. RLHF adds a KL penalty against a frozen reference. TRPO uses an explicit KL constraint.
cap.3: PPO has no KL term. TRPO maximises the surrogate subject to E[KL(π_old || π_θ)] ≤ δ; RLHF subtracts β·KL(π_θ || π_ref), with π_ref never updated. Different purposes.

chapters.name: The dead objective
chapters.title: Share of the batch past the clip band, epoch by epoch (illustrative)

cap.1: Study the same notes too many times and most of them stop counting. Learning goes quiet, which looks like being finished but isn't.
cap.2: Each extra epoch on one batch pushes more ratios outside the band, where they give zero gradient. Log the clip fraction: roughly 5-20% is healthy; past a third, stop.
cap.3: Symptom: return collapses and policy loss flatlines near 0 while advantages stay large. Fix: fewer update_epochs (4 is sane), fewer minibatch passes, a lower lr.

cap.1: This small rule made policy learning stable enough to become the default, and it is still what fine-tunes chatbots from feedback.
cap.2: RLHF and GRPO keep this exact clipped ratio and change what the reward and the baseline are. When you tune a language model with RL, this clip is in the loop.
cap.3: Knowing where gradient flows tells you how far one RL step can move a model's behaviour: the clip bounds per-batch drift, while RLHF's KL penalty bounds total drift.

caption.1: Pick a good or bad move and how wide the band is. Then slide the ratio: past the band on the too-eager side, the sample stops teaching anything.
caption.2: Good move (A above 0): flat past 1 + ε. Bad move: flat below 1 - ε. The gradient readout drops to exactly 0 there: removed, not shrunk. Widen ε and the flat part moves out.
caption.3: ∂L/∂r = A wherever the unclipped branch is the min (inside the band included) and 0 where the clipped branch wins. Clipping removes gradient; it does not rescale it.

hamming.what: PPO's objective: the probability ratio times the advantage, with the ratio clipped to [1-ε, 1+ε] and the smaller of the two taken.
hamming.when: In every PPO policy update, and so in RLHF and GRPO fine-tuning of language models.
hamming.why: It stops the policy over-learning from a batch it no longer resembles, giving TRPO-like stability with first-order gradients and a few lines of code.

object.title: The credit terraces
object.subtitle: Credit as a landscape over the ratio and the advantage, with flat terraces where the gradient is zero.

cap.1: The credit landscape. One edge is how much more often you now play a move; the other is how good the move was. Height is the credit.
cap.2: x: the ratio r. y: the advantage A. Height: min(rA, clip(r)A) with ε = 0.2.
cap.3: L_CLIP as a function of (r, A): piecewise linear, with plateaus where the clipped branch wins.

cap.1: On the good-move side the ground rises, then levels into a terrace past 1.2. Walking further earns nothing.
cap.2: For A above 0 the objective is flat for r beyond 1 + ε: no incentive to push the probability higher.
cap.3: ∂L/∂θ = 0 on the plateau: those samples contribute nothing to the update.

cap.1: On the bad-move side the terrace sits at the other end, below 0.8. One batch can't push a bad move's probability to zero.
cap.2: For A below 0 the objective is flat for r under 1 - ε: the penalty stops growing, so no crushing in one go.
cap.3: The clip is one-sided per sign of A: it removes gradient only in the direction that would exploit a stale estimate.

cap.1: Shrink the band and the terraces crowd in around ratio 1: tiny, cautious steps per batch.
cap.2: Small ε means most samples clip quickly: stable but slow.
cap.3: ε sets the per-batch trust region in ratio space; too small and the clip fraction saturates early.

cap.1: Widen it and the terraces retreat: bolder updates, and more risk of learning from notes that no longer describe you.
cap.2: Large ε allows bigger moves per batch, and more exposure to stale advantage estimates.
cap.3: As ε grows, L_CLIP approaches the unclipped surrogate, recovering vanilla importance-weighted policy gradient's instability.

predict.q: A good move's ratio has reached 1.5 with ε = 0.2. What gradient does this sample give?
predict.why: Past 1 + ε the clipped branch wins the min and does not depend on θ, so the gradient is exactly zero.

predict.q: Which algorithm uses an explicit KL constraint against the old policy?
predict.why: PPO clips the ratio; RLHF penalises KL against a frozen reference; TRPO constrains KL to the old policy.

predict.q: The clip fraction climbs past a third. First fix?

options.t: Fewer epochs per batch, or a lower learning rate
Raise ε so nothing gets clipped

predict.why: Most of the batch has gone stale; take fewer passes over it rather than silencing the alarm.
